Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is an honor to present the 2nd Voluntary National Review twin— of our Twin Island Federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Every VNR tells 2 stories. One is measured through policies and Programs and statistics. The other is measured through lives of people. Ultimately, it is the second story that matters most, and for that, as we would say in local Palance, we're doing something. 3 years ago, our Federation presented its first VNR to this Forum. Today we return with our second review, alongside the first voluntary local review for the Island of Nevis completed in 2025. Together, these reviews reflect our commitment to reporting progress and our belief that sustainable development requires us to pause, reflect honestly on where we have come from, learn from our experiences, and continually improve the way we serve our people. That philosophy is embodied in our Sustainable Island State Agenda, our homegrown development vision, and our National Development Planning Framework 2023 to 2037. Together, they have aligned the Sustainable Development Goals with our national priorities, ensuring that the 2030 Agenda serves as the blueprint through which we are shaping the future of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Today, I would like to share that story through 5 Sustainable Development Goals under review. For decades, reliable water supply remained one of our greatest development challenges. As one of the most water-scarce countries in the world, Saint Kitts and Nevis has long contended with the combined pressures of climate change, prolonged droughts, and limited freshwater resources, testing the resilience of our people year after year. Today, that story is changing. The commissioning of the 2 million gallon per day Bastyr Desalination Plant, made possible through the valued partnership and support of the Republic of China on Taiwan, in addition to the completion of a large water well in Cayonne, has increased the proportion of households on St. Kitts receiving 24-hour water service from just 25% a few years ago to nearly 70% today. Behind that statistic are thousands of families whose daily lives have been transformed. More families now have the confidence of knowing that reliable water will be available throughout the day, while we continue working to extend that same level of service to every community across our Federation. Businesses can operate with greater certainty. Communities are better equipped to withstand periods of drought. In fact, even as we are presently experiencing one of the worst droughts in our history, communities who long struggled with intermittent supply now have 24-hour water service. We're doing something. Our investment in water security has therefore become an investment in public health, economic resilience, and climate adaptation. Yet, our experience has also taught us, important lesson: resilience cannot be built one sector at a time. Water security depends upon energy security. For generations, the cost of electricity in Saint Kitts and Nevis has been shaped largely by forces beyond our control. Every fluctuation in global fuel prices affected households, businesses, and public services alike. Like many Small Island Developing States, we understood that our long-term prosperity could not remain tied indefinitely Complementing these investments is our Global Environment Facility Rapid Decarbonization Project, which is strengthening the policies, institutions, and technical capacity needed to support a cleaner and more resilient energy future. Colleagues, in a matter of just over 2 years from now, with our 50 MW solar PV plant and 30.5 MWh battery energy storage system coming on stream, St. Kitts would move from less than 2% renewable energy production to near 50% renewable energy penetration, even as this does not count the geothermal energy on the island of Nevis slated to be added to the grid in 3 to 4 years. We're doing something together. These initiatives are reducing vulnerability, strengthening economic competitiveness, and creating a more secure future for generations to come. They also demonstrate how one investment can advance multiple Sustainable Development Goals at the same time, supporting climate action, economic growth, and social well-being while reducing our dependence on imported fuels. Our approach to infrastructure has followed the same principle. For small island states, infrastructure is measured by whether it expands opportunity, strengthens resilience, and enables innovation. In the last 3 years alone, we have invested in roads that amount to 40% of the length of our entire main road of St. Kitts. At almost $100 million Eastern Caribbean dollars, that is around 10% of our national budget for a year. We're doing something. But perhaps nowhere is sustainable development more tangible than in the communities where people live, work, and raise their families. Creating sustainable communities means ensuring that development is felt not only in national statistics but in the everyday lives of our citizens. Through climate-smart housing initiatives, urban renewal programs, and the regularization of longstanding informal settlements, We are working to ensure that more families have access to safe housing, secure land tenure, and communities that are better prepared for the impacts of climate change. One moment remains particularly vivid in my mind. During the distribution of hundreds of land titles under our Squatter Regularization Initiative, one gentleman quietly shared how much that document meant to his family. He felt he had something now. He explained that he had already begun constructing an additional home on the same property for his grandson because, for the first time, he could plan with certainty for the generations that would follow him. We doing something. That conversation reminded me that sustainable development is ultimately about people. It is about creating opportunities that endure beyond our own lifetime. Sometimes the true impact of public policy cannot be measured in hectares of land or dollars invested, but in the hope it creates for the next generation. None of these achievements would have been possible through national effort alone. Like many small SIDS, Saint Kitts and Nevis continues to face significant challenges, including climate vulnerability, constrained access to concessional finance, and the need to strengthen national data systems to better inform decision-making. These realities remind us that international cooperation remains indispensable to sustainable development. Working alongside partners like the United Nations systems, the Green Climate Fund, the Saudi Fund for Development, the Republic of China and Taiwan, and our sisters and brothers across the African continent, we are strengthening institutions mobilizing investment, and building the national capacity needed to translate ambition into lasting results. These partnerships reinforce a simple but important truth: while development must always be nationally owned, it is most effective when supported by genuine international cooperation. Mr. President, our 2nd Voluntary National Review does not suggest that our work is complete. Rather, it reflects our determination to continue learning, adapting, and improving. But we're doing something. The Sustainable Development Goals have become deeply embedded within our Sustainable Island State Agenda because they speak to the future of our people, or the future that our people have chosen. A future where clean water is reliable, where energy is sustainable, where infrastructure is resilient, where communities are inclusive, and where partnerships enable even the smallest states— we are the smallest independent nation in the Western world— to pursue the biggest ambitions. The story of St. Kitts and Nevis is still being written, but Mr. President, we're doing something. We know that challenges remain, but we also know that progress is possible when national vision is matched by determined implementation and meaningful partnership. It is in that spirit that we reaffirm our commitment to the 2030 Agenda and to working with the international community to build a more resilient, more inclusive, and more sustainable future for all. St. Kitts and Nevis is doing something. I thank you.

For the first question, one of the key lessons from Somalia's development experience is that stronger institutions require stronger data. As our statistical system has developed, so too our ability to plan, monitor, and target our national priorities more effectively. Our progress has been guided by the Second National Strategy for Development of Statistics, which strengthens the national statistical system and reinforces the coordination role of the Somali National Bureau of Statistics across government. Given Somalia's context, we have adopted a practical approach to increasing data availability. While national representative surveys remain essential, they are resource-intensive and often depend on development partner support. At the same time, the Somali National Bureau of Statistics has worked closely with sectoral ministries to strengthen and digitize administrative data system is improving the availability of timely official statistics for SDG monitoring and evidence-based policymaking. These efforts are now supporting the implementation of Somalia's National Transformation Plan 2025, ensuring that progress towards inclusive growth and resilience is increasingly driven by reliable nationally audited data. This progress is also reflected internationally with Somalia's recording a significant improvement in the World Bank's statistical performance indicators from 19% in 2029 to 51% in 2024. Regarding the question from Bahrain, Somalia's economic progress has been built on sustained reforms and stronger national ownership. Over the past decade, we have implemented far-reaching reforms to strengthen public financial management, improve domestic revenue mobilization, and also reinforce macroeconomic stability. These efforts restored confidence in our economy and enabled Somalia to achieve the HIB completion bond, marking a major milestone in Somalia's economic recovery. However, we see this not as an end in itself, but as the beginning of a new phase of development. Alongside these reforms, We have strengthened the economic statistics needed to guide policy through the National— Somalia National Bureau of Statistics. We have expanded the production of key macroeconomic indicators, including the GDP and the consumer price indices, giving governments more timely and reliable evidence to monitor growth, inflation, and also the impact of economic reforms. Somalia has a long tradition of entrepreneurship, and our private sector has has demonstrated remarkable resilience despite decades of conflict. Therefore, our National Transformation Plan places private sector-led growth at the center of economic transformation. Our role as government is therefore to create an enabling environment where businesses can expand and also create jobs. A key part of the effort is the gradual formalization of the economy. The recent Business Establishment Census has, for the first time, time provided a comprehensive picture of Somalia's business landscape. This evidence is helping us design policies that encourage formalization, improve the investment climate, expand the tax base, and also unlock greater private sector. Our experience has shown that sustainable economic transformation is driven by sound economic reforms, strong institutions, and vibrant private sector with continued international partnership we are laying the foundation for inclusive growth, greater resilience, and also improved livelihoods for Somali people.
